observation: Refine and Design phases both skipped (backend-only refactor, no UI surface). Progress notes correctly identified the scope: 'gap already enumerated, infra only'. Skips appropriate — architecture-only WP with no new primitives. This sets a pattern: backend refactors with spec'd boundary contracts and no user-facing changes skip early phases and move straight to Phase 1 (architecture).

Phase-2 architecture-critique loop caught 2 real pre-build issues: (1) naming collision — proposed forwarder `harnessCapabilities` collided with the local response-body key in agent-profile.ts (AC-4 forbids renaming that shape), resolved to `harnessCapabilitiesForType`; (2) nullable-param mismatch — two call sites pass `AdapterPool | undefined` but forwarders typed non-optional. Reviewer independently found both against live code before builder wrote a line. Critique investment prevented build/fix/re-verify cycles.

Planner revised once (round 1→2) on both findings: renamed forwarder, added optional params with null/[] fallback to 2 of 6 forwarders. Reviewer re-verified and approved round 2. Single tight revision loop — findings were structural (not design-level disagreement), planner understood the scope immediately. This differs from multi-round explorations seen in other WPs; here the critique gates were sharp and findings were pin-point.

Phase 3 (build): green on first attempt. Implemented per plan exactly. All 121 tests pass (affected subset), npm run check 10 packages/0 errors, lint 6 guard scripts pass, knip production clean. No new lint violations, no type errors. 8 routes refactored to import from the new read-model, all call-sites rewired correctly (12 modified + 3 new files). Single-pass implementation suggests the architecture critique loop resolved ambiguities well enough that builder had a tight spec.

Phase 4 (code review): reviewer independently verified all 4 ACs against live code (not builder's self-report). Ran the guard script, confirmed AC-4 (guard prevents core→harness edges). Checked security lens — verified `Pick<AdapterPool,...>` genuinely omits all mutating/execution methods by structure, not by convention. Verdict: DONE, zero findings, first attempt. This tracks with AU12/AU13 pattern — clean pre-impl critique → zero review findings.

Lore capture strong: header comment in harness-capability-read-model.ts explains the AU16/AU11 co-guarantee (import boundary guard + structural Pick narrowing); au11-runtime-ownership-guard.ts AU16 doc comment (5 paragraphs) explains the DESCRIPTOR_READ_ALLOWLIST retirement and the new agent-owned sink model. Lore in code prevents future maintainers from re-introducing the old hand-verified pattern or misunderstanding the guard logic.

Guard pattern maturity: AU16 follows AU11 precedent (agent-owned-allowlist sink, moved forbidden boundary). Guard logic refactored cleanly — removed DESCRIPTOR_READ_ALLOWLIST hand-verified-file tracking, moved read-model to AGENT_OWNED_ALLOWLIST, simplified forbiddenEdge() logic (no more special-case type-only allow). The pattern is now internally consistent: any core→agent-owned edge goes through the allowlist sink, type-only or not. One less special case in the codebase.

AC-2 interpretation note: spec said 'one exported function', plan proposed 6 forwarders over a `Pick`-narrowed `HarnessCapabilityReader` type. Reviewer judged 6 functions (surface area = 6) over a narrowed type (structural guarantee) satisfies intent better than a literal single dispatcher. This pragmatic reading kept the API fine-grained (routes import exactly what they call) while maintaining the narrowing guarantee. Recorded in plan §5.3. No friction at build/review time because reviewer pre-approved the interpretation.

WP cost: refactor scope (8 routes + 1 guard script, ~11 files touched) + new service module (1 new, 1 new test) + testing (6 forwarders × tests + structural assignment + optional fallback tests). Phase 2 critique investment (~2h, 2 real findings) prevented a build-phase rework cycle. Total cost: ~1 day (architecture + critique loop + build + review). Mechanical nature + TDD structure (6 red tests written first) kept predictability high. Matches M complexity estimate.

guard-main.sh's PreToolUse hook blocks the CLAUDE.md-mandated worktree command itself: `git worktree add .worktrees/<id> -b <branch> origin/main` is rejected because Guard 1's regex `\bmain\b` matches the substring 'main' inside 'origin/main' (word boundary after '/'), not just a literal 'main' branch checkout. Every pipeline run creating a worktree off origin/main hits this false positive. Worked around this run via a throwaway local branch ref (`git branch -f au16-base origin/main` then `git worktree add ... au16-base`), but the underlying regex bug in .claude/hooks/guard-main.sh line 20 was NOT fixed. Recommend tightening the regex (e.g. anchor on whitespace/start-of-token before 'main', or exclude 'origin/main'/'refs/remotes/origin/main') so the canonical CLAUDE.md command stops false-positiving.

The ephemeral retro agent (fresh context, told to write to '.pipeline/retro-log/AU16.jsonl' inside the AU16 worktree) instead wrote the file to the PRIMARY checkout (/Users/tg/hyperidle/.pipeline/retro-log/AU16.jsonl) rather than the worktree path, requiring a manual move+cleanup by the orchestrator before shipping. Checking the primary checkout afterward found AU12.jsonl, AU13.jsonl, and AU14.jsonl ALSO sitting there as untracked files with zero git history anywhere (git log --all shows no commits touching them) — meaning three prior WPs' retro observations were silently stranded outside any worktree/PR and never made it to main. This is a 4-for-4 recurrence, not a one-off: the retro phase's file-path instruction needs to be unambiguous about worktree-relative-vs-absolute paths, or the orchestrator prompt needs to pass the worktree's absolute .pipeline/retro-log/ path explicitly rather than a relative one the agent can resolve against the wrong cwd.
